translations.text: Discourse of Saint John Chrysostom, bishop, on repentance, virginity and patience.
The blessed apostle Paul, apostle of the Gentiles and teacher of the churches, who forgot what had passed and what lay behind,
was straining forward. He had been clothed in this corruptible flesh and was hastening toward that incorruptible power,
"he who finished the course and kept the faith,"
"he who was dried up by fasting and tested in afflictions, who through hunger and thirst became pleasing to God,
"he who served Christ from Jerusalem as far as the West," who had Christ speaking with him: an angel on earth and a man of heaven, a distinguished apostle,
"with whom the Holy Spirit dwelt; and he ascended as far as the third heaven and heard those unspeakable words,
who dwelt in paradise together with his corruptible body," who was unrestrained in zeal, great in love and caring for the churches,
the preacher of piety and helper of the weak, leader of the faithful, reprover of the Jews and teacher of us all, and,
after death, teacher and preacher, who showed us how we ought to ascend to heaven.
If, then, such a man, who had found so much faith, who said:
"I know nothing of myself," was afraid and said: "Lest I preach to others and I myself be found unproven,"
what then shall we do, we who have not found the [?] of virtue at all?
Now we ought to keep vigil and pray at all times, and to ask of God not gold, nor silver,
nor indeed any other earthly wealth, but only the kingdom of heaven and to rejoice in the Lord.
Others rejoice in the riches of the earth, some in wine, and some in beauty and glory. But that virgin rejoices in the Lord, so that she may have praise from him and say:
"From you is my praise." Nothing is more shameless, nor more pitiable, than a wounded soul.
It is right to know what is good for the soul, and to speak through the Holy One:
"Lord, by your will give strength to my beauty," so that the bridegroom may see that righteousness of yours and say to you:
"You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you." But be careful, even if you acquire virtue.
Do not be exalted because of your beauty, lest because of your exaltation God turn away from you and rebuke you for your exaltation.
You are not able to endure as he endured for you: he humbled "himself" and bought you with his precious blood.
He who gives food to all flesh fasted for you. He who made the sweetness of honey drank gall for you.
He who crowned heaven with the multitude of stars put on a crown of thorns for you and "became obedient unto death."
Now, on account of all this, it is not rejoicing that is fitting, but weeping and mourning and trusting him who said:
"What you say in your hearts, repent of upon your beds." What we have done by day, let us destroy by night with sighing and tears.
"Thus Ahab repented and tore his garment, fasted and put on sackcloth, sighed and wept. And what did the Lord say to him?
'I will not bring his evil upon him.'" For this reason the Savior also said:
"Blessed are those who weep" — not for the dead, nor for anything else, but for sins, as David said:
"Every day I will wash my bed, and I will drench my couch with my tears," and again:
"Streams of water came down from my eyes, because I did not keep your law."
Wash away your defilement with tears, beat your breast and your forehead, and consider what you have sinned through being hunted and through sin.
You were hunted through your eye, "like David," for you wickedly opened your windows, and your eyes became enemies of your soul.
Close now with sighing those eyes that look wickedly, for the habit of sin casts the sinner into worse sin.
You are clothed in a holy garment; never sit down in an unclean place, lest you defile it.
If you disregard the first, the second and the third defilement, from then on your garment will be defiled, and do not be surprised even if it is altogether spoiled [?].
Nothing is as necessary as prayer, "lest you strike your foot against a stone," so that "the angel of God may encamp and deliver you," and you may be able to say:
"The angel of God delivered me from all evils," so that the angel of the Lord may call you as he called Abraham, for the angels love those who love their Lord.
"Take up a song and bring the timbrel, song and blessing with the lyre." You bring one, and three will be asked [?] of you;
let us stand by these three, as the Apostle said, so that "this body of ours, spirit and soul, may be made wholly perfect,"
so that this body of ours may be the timbrel, this spirit the song, and the soul the lyre. Over a timbrel they stretch the skin of a dead animal.
You too must put this body of yours to death, so that you may praise God as with timbrel and song. For he gave his own body to suffering for your sake.
See to it that he does not say: What profit to you is my blood? How are you worthy of it, you who thus gave up [?] being able and acting toward him?
You newly planted one, become a bearer of fruit, so that you may praise God. As much as you are able, so much fruit bring forth.
If you cannot bring forth the full hundredfold fruit, bring forth sixty; and if this too seems heavy and hard to you, bring forth only the third, which is thirty.
As much as you are able, so much bring forth, so that you may not be found fruitless and be cast into the fire. And if you have no gold and silver,
may you have holy deeds. And if you do not have even these, but wood, hay and reed, to be burned by fire, see that you do not make yourself into a pillar, which the Lord hated.
Jacob too made a pillar for Rachel, and the Lord did not hate it.
"See that your word does not stand before you like an idol on that fearful day of judgment and become your accuser."
Lest you then begin to be convicted without a witness and confess without anyone seeing. Consider what you have done and what you have said in foolishness.
Weep while there is time, so that you may not hear there and be told: "Have you come here to repent, where there is no time for repentance?"
While we have this time, let us do good. If we squander this time, we will not be able to find another.
For this reason Paul also teaches and says: "While we still have this time, let us do good."
Let us weep, since we have sinned; let us pour down our tears to the ground, let us beat our breasts, so that we may escape the gnashing of teeth there.
Let us weep "as David wept," so that we may become blessed.
Not only did he weep, but he also spent whole nights at it and drenched his bed with tears.
On one night he sinned and on all nights he wept. Thus it is right to confess: for He gave me eyes that I might see the light, but with them I have seen what is foul.
Let us strike at the eyes, for I looked with evil and opened my windows; for this reason I washed them with tears.
Thus it is right for all those who have looked with evil to wash their eyes with weeping. See the wound and recognize the healing. Guard the doors of the soul.
Not only the eyes, but also the ears and the mouth, for these are the windows through which either evil or good things enter.
Take care lest death enter through your window; rather, let your eyes always be for you fulfillers of the commandments and orders of God.
Then the mouth is for singing and for instruction in the Old and New Law.
It is right to open those windows toward God and to shut them against sins. Then you too should say with that Holy Spirit, as he said:
"How shall I climb the ladder, take hold of its height and its righteousness, and love it, which [?] has a pure heart? From there I shall ascend to heaven and no longer do anything of the earth."
See, for the palm tree [?] is also thorny and a reprover of sins, for it is said of the words of the wise:
"They are like goads and like red-hot nails, so that by them we may be pricked and our hearts may be bent and depart from all sins."
But take hold of its height by means of it, so that you may always stand without falling and endure the coming winds, which are the temptations of the demons that come from time to time.
Devote yourself always to those divine books. As someone drinks wine, ceases from thirst, and is turned to joy,
so also whoever drinks that spiritual wine, his soul will be turned to joy. Remember God always and say with the holy one:
"I saw the Lord beforehand; He is always before me, for He is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken."
Write these words with your hand, and let them be unshaken before your eyes.
If you honor God, He will stand at your right hand; if you do not honor Him, "the devil will stand at your right hand,"
[?] ..., for in this way Judas dishonored the Lord, and the scripture was fulfilled in him that says:
"Let the devil stand at his right hand." At all times glorify God and say: "I will exalt you, O God, my King."
Fulfill this by deeds and not by words, for in this way David also blessed the Lord forever.
not for one month only, nor for one season, nor for one year, but at all times, for he knew that when a person has finished,
Only then let him begin. And if you say, "How can the heart always exalt God, as Paul did?" he writes:
"I know nothing against myself." David was the same, and he said: "Cleanse me from my secret faults."
This is what the Savior also commanded us, saying: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."
So the one who does not sin exalts God day by day, not only in word, but also shows it plainly in deed.
He is the one who does not become faint-hearted, even if suffering comes upon him, or anything else, or death; but say with Paul:
"Who will separate us from that love of Christ?" and what follows.
Christ does not dwell in a defiled house, but in the heavens, so prepare your soul as a dwelling place for him.
Remember the trembling and the terror of that day, when we are all to stand before him and give an account for each of our deeds.
Then sin will be set before the eyes of all and revealed to all, and those who do not know God will then be shown where the river of fire is, and the many-colored worm.
Then we will all stand naked and with bowed necks, where the books of our hearts will be opened and read out before many, things manifest and hidden,
of night and of day and of all times, the follies and the forgetfulness that our members have committed.
Then we will understand that revelation, for the things now hidden will be revealed.
Then we will understand that we must go before that great Judge, where not only for deeds
but also for words and desires he will judge us, where, though someone may suppose his errors to be small, this terrible judgment is going to come.
Always remember and do not forget the furnace that will never be extinguished.
Always keep before your eyes the one who is coming to judge the living and the dead.
Consider the thousands and myriads of angels standing before that Judge.
Then your ears will hear the cry of that trumpet and the terrible voice of the Judge.
Let your eye see beforehand the time when he will hand some over to that outer darkness, and when the door of the kingdom will be shut against others.
After their great virginity and labor, they will see some being bound like tares and laid in the furnace, and some being bound hand
and foot and led to the outer darkness, and some being handed over to the unceasing worm, and some being handed over to the gnashing of teeth.
Now consider: some will be punished for untimely laughter, and those who harmed a neighbor or led a brother astray;
some will be punished for unfathomable sins, some will enter torment for an idle word, and some for knowledge
will be punished; for some the kingdom of heaven will be shut because of blasphemy, and some will suffer unceasingly because of remembering wrongs.
Some stand in eternal shame, and some will be found lacking in knowledge, and they will hear:
"I do not know you, who you are, because you did what Christ did not command to be done."
Know that this is how it will be. How then shall we be, or what do you think? For, out of our earnestness, let us pour down tears like rivers
let us pour them down and say: "Who will give my head water, and my eyes a fountain of tears,
that I might weep for my sins day and night?" so that we may escape those coming torments.
"Come, let us hasten before his face with confession and with the repentance of this world,
and let us find forgiveness of sins from the Lord, for it is said: "In hell who will confess you?"
God has given us everything in twos: two eyes and two ears, two hands and two feet, and if one of these is harmed, we may be comforted in our need by the other;
but one soul has been given to us. If we destroy it, with what then shall we be saved?
Let us take thought for this alone, and let us count nothing as greater than its life,
for it too is to be judged, and is to render an account, and is to stand with us before the tribunal of God.
If you then say, "Wealth enticed me," the Judge will answer you and say to you:
"Have you not heard: What profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his own soul?"
If you say, "The devil led me astray,"
that word did not profit even Eve, for she said, "The serpent led me astray."
Let us now keep all this in our mind; come, let us set ourselves upright before the darkening and the coming of that day,
great and manifest, of which the prophet said: "Behold, that day is coming, and who will endure its coming?"
Terrible is that day, that day of fog and darkness. But you say: how then is there deliverance from these evils spoken of before?
Now I tell you: not that you should keep your flesh pure, but when you suffer evil, then it will profit you, and when they accuse you, reflect.
If anyone reviles you, bless him; and when you fast, do not become proud.
Fasting does not mean abstaining from foods; rather, it brings about the forgiveness of sins. It is right to look into the books:
"Now see how the prophet first saw the rod of walnut, and then the boiling [?pot], and he shows
that those who did not endure the rod were burned in the fire."
"So too Moses showed at that time the pillar of fire: those who listened to the law saw light, and those who did not listen remained in the fire."
Read the teaching of the Savior and learn that when you pass from this world, no one is able to help you.
Neither will brother rescue brother from those unceasing torments, nor friend friend, nor parents their children, nor a child his parents; and what shall I say of other people?
Not even them any longer [?], and "if Noah and Job and Daniel should come"; but I shall say: where does this showing of theirs come from?
"Now see the one who was not wearing the wedding garment, how he was thrown out of the wedding, and no one was found to intercede for him.

"Now see the one who was entrusted with the [?] (the text reads 'firebrand'; apparently the talent is meant) and did not trade with it, how he was given over to the darkness, and no one pleaded for him."
"Now see the five virgins, for whom the door was shut, and their own sisters did not intercede for them, the ones whom Christ also called foolish.
After the trampling down of the furnace of desire, after the quenching of that burning desire, by fasting and vigil and lying on the ground,
even then the name given to them was foolish and not righteous, for they preserved that great virginity but did not keep even a little love of humankind.
"Now see the Judge, how he sets the sheep on his right and the fruitless goats on his left.
On that day of judgment he will say to those on the right: Come and inherit the kingdom of heaven,
but those on the left he will hand over to the outer darkness, and no one will be able to help them.
True is the one who said: Behold, the man and his deeds.
"You have surely heard of the rich man who did not have mercy on Lazarus the poor man, how he burned in that place of torment and longed for a drop of water to drink.
Understand that not even Abraham himself, who pleaded for the people of Sodom, became his deliverer from those torments."
Now therefore, from this time on, let us help ourselves and give glory to God before darkness falls.
It is better that we dry up our tongue here by fasting than that we fail to keep the commandment and long for a drop of water, and it is not brought there, but one is tormented unceasingly.
Through the small suffering of this world let us escape great torment.

Let us understand that we cannot endure the heat of even three days, and that we would look upon the tortures of the judges and melt away, and this torment lasts, even if it were so long, fifty years.
How much greater, then, will that torment of God be, not only fifty years, but a torment incomprehensible and prolonged for ever.
"At all times, now, let us enter by the narrow gate, so that we may walk on those broad roads."
Let us know that all these things of this world are like a vision and a dream, and are subject to the generation of corruption.
Even if we have strength of body, sickness corrupts the flesh and old age melts away beauty.
If we refresh ourselves with food at table, night comes and destroys everything, for all this is a passing shadow, unstable and deceptive like a dream.
For this reason the Savior calls the afflicted blessed, so that good foods may not deceive the one who eats. Now, as Abraham heard:
"Go out from your land," so now let us also go out from habit, so that by that training in our way of life we may come to dwell in the heavenly city.
"Let us strengthen these bodies of ours by fasting and enslave them," so that we may not enslave souls and bodies to the devil.
By all means, by that training of spiritual psalmody let us come to dwell in the heavenly city, and those desires of ours,
As with wild beasts, let us lull [them] to sleep with vigil, psalms and hymns.
Let us always strip away [?] the settled ease of our bodies. Let us remember the one who said: "Be watchful and stand vigilant."
No one who is asleep becomes crowned, nor does one who lies down and snores receive honor; rather, the one who is covered in dust and wounded,
such a one will be found among the perfect, who endures the battering [?] of his brain and shows the blood flowing down.
For we have learned by experience that the devil's scheming is hard and harsh: it flees from the watchful and plunders those who sleep.
Give no sleep to your eyes and no slumber to your eyelids, so that you may be saved like a gazelle from the net and like a bird from the snare.
Let us always flee from the snares of this world and from the tares,
and let us act as though we had left this world, and let us not strive at all for the flesh, for the ambushes of the deceiver are many. For it is said:
"Our enemy, like an enraged lion, roars, runs to and fro, and seeks not merely to bite
or to tear apart, but to swallow him up completely." Flee from the schemes of the deceiver and say:
"For by you I shall be delivered from temptation, and by my God I shall leap over a wall." Do not flee from labour, so that the crown may not flee from you.
Just as a merchant does not grow weary but takes labor upon himself in order to gain wealth, so let the good and brave man endure wounds, for he sees the crown.
A laborer will not find a harvest unless he has first sown the seed with his own labor and sweat.
So too, those who look toward heaven count tribulation as nothing, for they are strengthened by that sweet hope.
From now on let us always keep watch and wait for when the Bridegroom comes from the wedding, so that we may hear his voice and rise ready to meet him, and he may say to us:
"Blessed are you, men, who wait for the Lord." Here too the Saviour calls the watchful blessed and says:
"Blessed is that servant whose lord shall come and find him awake."
Just as he calls the watchful blessed, so too he reproaches the negligent and says:
"If that evil servant begins to say, 'My lord delays his coming,' and begins to beat and mistreat his fellow servants, and eats and drinks with the drunkards,
that lord of his will arrive on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him apart and assign his portion with the unbelievers."
Behold, the one who said, "He will delay," is cut apart; and the one who was not expecting him who is to come, why does he suffer this harm?
we ought to stand ready and prepared to depart from this world, and to say always:
"My heart is ready toward you, O God." We are in a great battle in this world: "the ungodly walk round about,"
"the sinners have bent their bow." At some they shoot at the ears, so that they may listen to evil speech; at some they shoot at the eyes,
so that they may look and stir up desire with evil; at some he shoots at the tongue, so that he may revile his brothers;
at some he shoots at the belly, so that they may be gluttonous; at some he shoots at the hands, so that they may be robbers; at some he shoots at the feet,
so that they may walk in evil, those whom he shoots in the heart, so that such a person may be greedy and envious and rancorous and a doer of every evil.
For this reason Paul also arms us with that spiritual armor and writes:
"Take up that armor and helmet, so that we may be able to quench all the fiery arrows of the enemy."
Let us believe the voice of the prophet, as he said:
"If you have heard, O man, what the Lord seeks from you: only that you do justice and love mercy and walk in readiness with the Lord your God."
Now let us forget what lies behind and stand firm, so that we may eat the fruit of our labor and take delight from the Lord.
Let us not waste our times in vain. We have our own Lord, so that we may show our servitude toward him.
He admonishes us and reminds us and testifies to us and rebukes, he comforts us and teaches us, and as a reward for obedience he grants us the kingdom.
Gird your waists with truth, and let us serve the good Lord and let us suffer, just as the Savior suffered for us, as he was born for us,
ate and drank, slept and rose and was baptized; they reviled him, he trembled, he was distressed, he was beaten, he was insulted, and in this way [?] he took death upon himself.
Truly consider him who thus endured the lawless ones on account of our sins, those who rose up against him, and who resisted sin even to death and fought against it.
How many things he did for us: he healed the sick, raised the dead, cleansed lepers, cast out demons,
made the lame walk, and after this he granted us ascent to heaven, so that we too may follow him by that virtue of life and attain that heavenly life.
"For our stay in this world is for a short time, but it is in that age that our life is to be,
where the Lord has promised us, for Scripture has called us strangers and pilgrims in this world, so that we may despise what is here."
The desire of this world is like a dog: if you drive it away, it flees from you; if you feed it, it stays with you.
For this reason James also said: "Resist the devil and he will flee from you." Let us not wait for hell, where the medicine of repentance is of no use.
Even if someone gnashes his teeth and his tongue burns with fire, no one will moisten it for him even with a drop of water on a finger, but there he will hear what that rich man heard.
Know now that this world is like a dream and that we are staying as if in an inn, and departure from here lies before us.
Let us take care for the road and the provisions for eternal life; let us carry them with us ourselves [?].
Let us put on the garment that is to be taken away with us, about which Paul spoke to us: "mercy, compassion, sweetness and holiness."
There we need not gold but dew, not leaves but fruit, not words but deeds;
"Not those who say to me: Lord, Lord, but those who do my will."
Now let us not deceive ourselves, even if we give ourselves up and are wholly zealous for that life.
What can be compared to that age? In this world both good and evil have an end, but there the torments are unceasing.
Here, if the flesh burns, the soul departs; but there the resurrection of the flesh will be incorruptible, and the soul will burn forever,
for sinners too are to rise incorruptible, not so that they may be honored, but so that they may be tormented without dying.
If we cannot even bear the harsh, burning air of the baths, what shall we do there, at that river of fire? For "we are all to be tested by fire."
If the gold is one's own, one ought to look at the seal, lest the treasure be lost. One ought to examine whether what is hidden is really as what is manifest.
We shall all stand naked and with bowed necks before him to whom this account is due, and there is no one who will escape the wrath of that Judge.
But if you say: How can the soul be able to burn forever?
Just as here bodies are in fever and burn, and when the flesh grows weak here, the soul expires.
But there the soul will not grow weak, but will go on burning together with the flesh.
Is there anyone now who, for the sake of a dream, would want eternal torment? Or how can it be a fair exchange for what we await?
If everything that passes away is thus, how will that which is enduring be?
While we have this time, come, let us heal these wounds of our souls with tears, and let us not spread out our hands on our own behalf and yet stand upon the very same things.
"If one builds and another tears down, what profit is there, except only vain labour?"
And if Jeremiah lamented over that temple of stone when it was destroyed, and said:
"Leave me alone, so that I may weep bitterly; do not press me with consolation."
how much more ought one to weep for the soul, where not golden jars, but the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit dwell?
If we are grieved for the dead, who is so unfeeling that his soul should have died and he would not weep?
He who heals the body kills his own soul, but he who has taken pains for souls has not healed his own body.
Now let us shed tears not for the dead, but for ourselves.
Let us remember that day, for it is the time of the end, and that Judge has arrived at the doors.
Even if he were far off, not even so would it be right to be without fear. "That night has come; now let us awaken from dreams."
Even if this passing repose is lovely, it is nothing more than a dream, and one who sees the sun ought not to fall asleep.
"Let us worthily produce the fruit of repentance," for it is written. Just as washing with water is easy,
so too is cleansing the soul by repentance easy. The martyrs did not entreat God at all times, but in a single hour they were crowned.
If that sin of yours is unforgivable and you sin even until death, we have a saving medicine, if we do not ourselves cut off our hope,
for nothing is so hard for the fallen as not rising; for the sin of man is not rising [?], but to fall and no longer rise, and death, belong to the devil alone.
Just as our good Lord cries out through the prophet: "Is there no medicine in Gilead? Or are there no physicians there?"
If anything harms this flesh, we beseech physicians, turn to medicines, and set everything in motion,
so that we may heal that sick member of ours; but when the soul is harmed, we are negligent and do not exert ourselves for it even in word.
"Let us fear him who is able to destroy soul and body in that Gehenna of fire."
Now, before the time of torment comes, let us come and fall into the abyss of his mercies, and say with holy David:
"Wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow." Our good Shepherd stands and wishes to snatch us from the mouth of the lion before we are swallowed up.
He cries out now and says to us: Child, have you sinned? Do not add to it any more. "Shall the one who falls not rise again?
Or shall the one who turns away not return?" "Return to me, you apostate sons, and I will heal those wounds of yours."
He who said this does not lie: "I did not come to judge this world, but to save it."
"Only let us repent, for he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and be saved."
How could a man love and have mercy on his wife in this way, as much as God does the soul that repents?
Her who has sinned he invites, and after all this he says to her: "Return to me!"
So innumerable are the Lord's acts of love for mankind, and he casts away no one at all of those who turn to him, but stretches out his hand and says to them: "Today, if you will hear my voice."
"If a physician is often reviled by the one who is being treated by him, and he does not despise him because of the reviling,
but brings in still greater helpers and counts that mind [?] of his as nothing, how much more will the Lord, the physician of our souls, be merciful to us?
Only let us not cut off our hope, for a champion often falls and in the end becomes crowned.
A soldier is often wounded, is healed, rises again, and is found more experienced through that fall.
Finally, many merchants lose their money and then grow rich by labor; they trade again after the loss, and by their labor they win back greater wealth.
Did he perhaps prepare the fire for us? God forbid! It was for the devil and his servants. But we ourselves have kindled the fire, and we have heard:
"Walk in the light of your fire and in the furnace that you have kindled." There is no affliction that the physician's medicine cannot heal.
But what shall I say? I am not able to show a complete conversion.
If you are not able to be like the sun, become like the moon.
If you cannot be the moon, become like a star. Only rise up from the earth and begin to resemble those lights of the stars.
It is better that you have a little amendment than complete separation.
"God has set a cool drink before you, so that you may look after the sick," and may you see those in prison.
"If judgment is to be rendered for words and desires, how much more, if we do righteousness, shall we not lose our reward?"
Even if the matter is something small, now, from this time on, strive a little for one hour, so that we may not fall away from those eternal good things.
If [?] whatever death should come, we ought to endure it, so that we may see Christ coming in his glory, and see the King not from afar, but face to face.
If here we marvel at the beauty of this flesh, which is ash and dust and worm, how shall we not be far more amazed if we see those things of the incorruptible one?
Peter saw only a small light of his glory and said: "It is good for us to be here."
What then shall we say, we who are in any case waiting to see that immortal King, if not [?] those who stand before the king,
we call blessed those whom we see with the high golden seat, the belt and the crown.
How then shall we be, we who are to stand before him who is coming to judge the earth?
If the king were summoning you, and the road were harsh, or infested with robbers and very terrifying, would you not undertake everything?
Do not say, "I am held fast by sin and I cannot turn to God." David too fell, and so he rose again and became a teacher to his children.
If the devil has tripped you, let us rise up by ourselves, and the Lord will come to meet you and will receive you as his son.
Understand that after kingship and luxury, after planting and building and every work, Solomon said:
"Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." If those who are [?] singers and slaves were to praise us,
robbers and petty men, would we not strive in every way to seize that praise?
And where angels and archangels will judge us at that [?] sight, what shall we do for them,
"Will harlots and tax collectors go before us into the kingdom of heaven?" In the books there are testimonies that support one another:
"Ahab repented and gained mercy by that medicine"; "the Ninevites, by fasting";
"Belshazzar escaped slaughter by almsgiving"; "the harlot washed the feet of the Lord with tears";
Paul "confessed his sins and became a teacher of the penitent"; "the thief believed and inherited the kingdom."
Let us find this medicine and heal our wounds ourselves, and let us say:
"Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; have mercy on my soul," "for I have sinned against you." That physician will receive us and will say to us:
"I am, I am he who blots out your sins, and I will remember them no more." See how many medicines that physician has mixed for you.
Choose whatever you wish; how many different kinds he has shown you for your many wounds!
If you are not able to show mercy like Belshazzar, repent like Ahab.
If you are not able to fast like the Ninevites, wash away your sins with your tears like that harlot.
If you are not able to fast and to confess your sins, flee to the merciful one and say with David:
"Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy," for it is not a viper's bite, that you should apply medicine to it.
Nor is it stained with mud, that I might wash it off with water.
It is the bite of the devil. O Lord, we beseech your mercy and your love for mankind. But let us turn back and fall down fervently before him, so that he may kindle his mercy upon us, he who said:
"If the lawless one turns back from his evil way, I will no longer remember all the iniquities that he has committed."
But confess your passions and say: "Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me; have mercy on my flesh and my soul:
have mercy on me here and in the age to come as well; have mercy on this weak nature of mine by your goodness."
But may you long for healing, for that physician seeks your life, he who brought back the sheep that had gone astray, he who sent out three times to call the wicked and the good.
Behold, he is selling you the kingdom of heaven. If you do not have the price to buy it, buy it with a sigh and a piece of bread.
Gain the kingdom of heaven for yourself. Behold, the prophet cries out and says:
"Who wishes to buy life, and who is it that wishes to see good days?"
You who have no silver, receive without silver. What does he seek from you? Who is this who is selling to you?
Do you have no price, neither repentance, nor fasting, nor tears, nor anything else that is required?
"Restrain your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit," and that is enough for your salvation.
See that if you fast, you do not become exalted. If you have shown mercy to someone, do not boast.
But when the fast has passed, then consider what you have gained in that fasting, lest you come out just as you went in.

See which sin you have put away from yourself, or what better thing you have found, or what good you have gained, or what deficiency you have cast off, whether you have ceased from anger or from reviling;
whether you have not spoken evil about your brother; whether you have ceased from hot temper; whether you have done some other good.
If you have only abstained from foods and have done no other good deed, that fast will be of no benefit to you,
but you have subjected your belly in vain, and it will answer you and say to you: Well, were you not able to fast? Why did you not stand against your enemy?
Why did you persist in attacking [?] and in envy? Or why did you become angry at the one who afflicted you?
Not only this, but if you persist in remembering wrongs, than which no evil is worse; for the fornicator,
or the adulterer, did evil at one time and quenched his desire, but the one who remembers wrongs commits sin both day and night and at every hour.

If you remember this, you will never think of reviling; and if someone has reviled you and you have reviled him, the one who commanded you [?], for at that visitation of the world all this is to be revealed.
Now, before being cast down into that pit of destruction, let us flee from such torment.
Let us understand that no one is able to deliver us from that torment.
Neither Moses, nor Noah, nor Daniel, nor even Abraham himself, the lover of his children, will redeem us from that torment.
Let us understand that we are under many sins, both manifest and hidden, as it is said:
"If you repay me according to my iniquities, O Lord, O Lord, who could withstand you?"
And what shall we say about those hidden sins, if he should exact from us a reckoning for the manifest ones?
How shall we find forgiveness, if he should judge us for negligence in prayer, or for faintheartedness in fasting?
When we stand before him, what shall we say, or what shall we plead?
For we do not give him so much honor: neither as servants give their own lord, nor as peoples give the ruler they are under, nor even as friends give a friend.
We speak with a friend with much reverence, yet we entreat God about our sins and are negligent.
Your knees lie on the ground and your mind wanders about. If he should wish to judge for this, where shall we hide?
If he should set before us accusers of what we do to one another, if he should judge us for wandering of mind and search out our evil thoughts,
if he should exact a reckoning from us for a word of blasphemy, how shall we be able to open our mouth?
If he judges us for boasting in prayer and fasting and almsgiving, how shall we be able to lift our eyes to heaven?
If he judges us for what we say to one another about servants, and because when a brother comes,
we speak with him as with a friend, and when he has gone away from us we speak evil of him, what torment shall we enter for this?
What if he judges us for swearing and lying and error, or for groundless anger?
What if he should reckon against us swearing falsely, or the grief with which we have distressed our brothers, or those who were suffering evil and whom we disregarded?
If he should exact from us a reckoning for those times of our negligence, because he himself speaks to us from the Scriptures,
but we left him and talked with our companions, what torment shall we enter for this?
Now torment is always before our eyes. Even if the torment is simple [?], how much more so for those who have grown accustomed to this?
It is proper to remember one's own sins. Remember the Judge. Behold, I tell you of the torment beforehand, so that you may flee from that affliction.
If he says to you, "Fast," you plead weakness as an excuse; if he speaks to you of almsgiving to the poor, you plead poverty as an excuse;
if he says to you, "Guard your mind from wandering," you make excuses about everything.
If he says to you, "Do not be angry," what will you answer to this, where neither weakness, nor poverty, nor affliction hinders you from practicing virtue?
Because of this your sins are unforgiven. How are you able to stretch out your hands to heaven?
Or how do you move your tongue and ask for forgiveness? Have you been harmed and deprived, and have you heard evil spoken of you and been greatly harmed?
Wait for the command of the ruler. When a servant insults you, you do not strike him, but accuse him to his own master; how much more should you do so with him who said:
"Vengeance is mine and I will repay, says the Lord." If you fast from food, see what sin you have put away from yourself,
or what better thing you have found, or what righteousness you have acquired, or what deficiency you have cast off.
Know now that you are going to stand before the throne, where excuses are of no profit,
nor does strength have any power, nor are witnesses of any help, for our soul is to pass through fire.
Send forth the drops; let the springs of tears be stirred. You have a well: from that depth of the heart draw them up with anguish.
Stir both pupils of your eyes and make tears flow down like rivers; as much as you have sinned, so much also shed tears.
If you have sinned little, a little tear is enough; if the sin is great, let your tears be more than a river.
If you have acquired purity, pour out tears for another and weep for a sinful brother, and see to it that you shed tears always for your own sins.
From where the sin came forth, let that spring be the healing, and before that door is shut let us repent.
Where the sin is, there also let the forgiveness be. Let it not be that the sin is here and the repentance in heaven.
"He has authority on earth to forgive sins": the Savior who has redeemed us.
"Let those who think they are standing take heed, lest they fall." Let the one whose feet have stumbled look to rising again, and let the one who falls only not be shattered.
If anyone has been shattered, there is one who raises up the fallen. There is also a slight [?], as holy David says:
"A little more and my steps would have slipped," and I said:
"My feet have stumbled, and your mercy, O Lord, helped me." And there is a leaning over and not a falling.
"I was forced to lean over so as to fall, and the Lord took me by the hand." And there is consolation even for the one who has fallen, so that he may not simply remain in sin.
"Shall the one who has fallen not rise again?" For God, the lover of mankind, is the one who raises up the fallen, as it is written:
"And the Lord raises up all the fallen." But take care, and do not become negligent, and hope in that good One.
"God is a righteous judge, mighty and long-suffering and a lover of mankind, and he always waits for repentance.
If you do not turn back, his sword is sharpened and does not yet cut, but he only sharpens it, so that you may see and not fall into torment."
He does not merely cut, but frightens, so that the fear of him may drive you into repentance.
He has drawn his bow and does not shoot, so that he may frighten you with the sight of it. The judge is ready; and do not despise that bow, for it flies.
Do not grow weak because you do not yet see his arrow, nor be negligent because of his long-suffering.
Hear the voice of the Savior, how he said: "Be wise and gentle toward your enemy and with your enemy."
You travel the road day by day, and you cannot, as it were, flee from him.
Paul writes and says: "The flesh fights against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, and it opposes the spirit", that hope for which we always wait.
He writes and lays down ordinances concerning the desire of the world and concerning the kingdom of heaven.
This flesh is bent toward the earth, but the spirit strives to become like the image of God.
So be prudent toward the enemy, while you are with him on the road in this world.
If the road comes to its end, there is no longer any time for repentance. Take care that the enemy does not hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the servants,
who are able to torment you and cast you into prison and into that outer darkness, until you pay that last stamped coin.
Not only for deeds, but for desire too one will be judged.
All this we know, and [?] ourselves. Only then shall we understand how bitter desire is, when we are put to the test: how much bitterness does it deceive us into?
So let us know now where we stand, and let us beseech the merciful God not to hand us over to the devil, and let us say with holy David:
"Do not hand me over to those who harm me", for they rouse us to sin, and those same ones become our accusers.
Not only will the devil alone open his mouth against us, but many devils, and they will say:
"Did you not become servants to us in anger and envy and boasting and pride and evil speech against a brother?"
Now let us be afraid of that day when our own thoughts become bitter adversaries at law against us.
Let us not wait for false witnesses, but rather let us beseech God.
Even though these bodies of ours that we wear are weak, yet great is he who is able to help us and give us life in his kingdom.
It is right to love one's own Lord, the beautiful and long-suffering, who loves his own servants. We humans too love certain people for these three reasons:
either for their goodness, or for profit, or if they are some of our own kin. What, then, is more beautiful than our Lord?
As David said: "He is fairer in appearance than the sons of men." Who is so beneficial,
"he who has prepared for those who love him what eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and what has not entered into the heart of man"?
And has anyone else loved us as much, as God our Father in his goodness cries out with love and speaks thus:
"A woman may perhaps forget her adornment, but I will not forget, says the Lord."
This one David loved, and he longed to see him and said: "When shall I come and appear before the face of God?"
He did not allow himself time until tomorrow, but burned with longing to depart from this world, so that he might see that Desired One.
The wisdom of the soul is understanding, which flies upward. You too should long for this.
Everything that you see passes away like a shadow, and may you always remember that eternal life and the kingdom that does not pass away,
To be with the angels and unaging glory, to dwell with Christ and to be separated from all afflictions.
Understand that this world has nothing except tears [?] reproach and reviling, [?] and pain, disease and old age, sin and death.
David saw all of this: slander, widowhood, poverty, suffering, torment, guilt. His heart longed to leave these things behind, and he spoke thus:
"When shall I come and appear before the face of God," so that I may depart to where there is peace, joy, love,
long-suffering, radiance, freedom from care, and other good greater than this, which we are unable to express.
And now you, who think of rest and luxury, do not despise your life.
If the one you despise were someone small or poor, you might well have slept.
If he whom we await is radiant and glorious and Lord of the whole world, let your light shine day by day and be ready to meet him, so that you may hear:
"Enter into the joy of your Lord."
Now it is fitting to keep vigil and to pray at all times. If God said to the devil:
"Do not touch Job," yet he went and thought to tempt him [?]
how much more will he fight against us, who are under his hands, as he wishes. Vigilance is always needful for everyone.
The athlete never sleeps on a bed, but on the ground, so that he may stay wakeful.
The fisherman does not sleep, but stands upright and is watchful all night.
The laborer is wakeful every day, so that no one may come into his lord's vineyard and ruin it. So it was with Jacob, who said:
"I was consumed by the heat of the day and the frost of the night, and sleep departed from my eyes";
and there is nothing to compare with his vigilance, so that not even one sheep should become food for the wild beasts.
If there is so much toil over irrational sheep, how much more over the rational soul?
It is right that one should always labor for the soul, which is more precious than the whole world,
which is coming with us, and is to give account and to stand before the throne of God.
For this reason "Jacob, while fasting, placed a stone as a pillow and slept, so that he might see the true stone in a vision,
just as he saw a ladder raised up as far as heaven and the angels of God descending and ascending,
who carried up our prayer and brought down grace and mercy from the Lord.
That valiant man did not anoint himself with ointment, for such is the zeal of the virtuous.
Nothing is more defiling to the soul than when the body has such a fragrance,
but just as when some [?] comes out of our bodies and runs down from our head onto our garment, and it is filled with uncleanness,
So too from the soul that has flowed out unclean from that flesh, the stench becomes perceptible.
The one who has grown wanton in this world and provokes anger indulges himself [?] in desire, whatever desire he has.
"The one who sleeps on a bed of ivory," and if it is of silver, has all the more earthly toil and will obtain wrath from heaven.
Our other sins involve some desire, but the one lying on that silver bed has some luxurious pleasure.
As the prophet reproaches their dissoluteness and says:
"who lie upon beds of ivory and defile their bed upon them."
Do you wish to see a royal bed, one that is full of virtue?
See David, the prophet, whose tears were like pearls,
"how day by day he drenched his couch," which was written as a sign for us, so that we too may follow in his footsteps and flee from the judgment to come.
Now, before the judgment, let us rid ourselves of all our guilt. There you will have no power to repent. He wants us to be ready.
For this reason too he left our departure from this world unrevealed, so that we may always be in supplication and labor.
For if here, when people hear the judges and the voice of the heralds, those who are about to be brought before the judge tremble and are out of their minds with fear,
how much more should we, who are to stand before that tribunal of God?
28. Let us marvel greatly in silence, and may the mind be pricked continually, all the more when I speak to you about the judgment; and now this reproof by words is good.
Yes, if that rich man too had been reproved, his tongue would not have burned there. Did your heart desire virginity? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will guard it.
If you say in prayer, "Guard me, Lord, as the pupil of the eye," he will answer and say to you:
"Keep my commandments and live, and my words as the pupils of the eyes."
When you walk in this way, he will seek out your care and say to you: "Whoever touches you, how would anyone touch the pupil of his own eye?"
Now you have put your hand to the plow; do not turn back, so that you do not become a pillar of salt.
Let your tongue always speak about the judgment [?]; say nothing better than that, neither in anger nor in grief nor with any other passion, but rather speak about the torment there,
so that it may profit you in that dark torment. And let the law of God always be in your mouth, so that the words and laws of God may come forth from your mouth.
Keep the Lawgiver always before your eyes. Let him be your home and your counselor; make him a member of your household and your companion in conversation.
If you see someone living in pleasure, or in luxury, or in power and at ease, understand that they will quickly wither like grass.
He takes his delight in food, but you, take your delight in the Lord.
Many virgins were martyred. If they overcame death, how are you, a man, unable to subdue desire?
Put your members to death, not only with regard to desire: also bear with resentment and anger, and let your tongue keep to measure.
See that your mind does not perhaps condemn you before the time.
"Death is coming and everything will be revealed." Here you do not want to be shamed before one person; and there, before those myriads, where shall we hide?
John was holy, and for this reason he leaned upon the Lord's breast. The soul that wishes to be pleasing to Christ must preserve purity,
"so that the tree may be known by its fruit." The righteous one declares the demonstration of faith.
Always remember this good confession, and keep in your mind that day of the end.
See that you are not perhaps corrupted by the tongue, for it is said: "The tongue defiles the whole body."
When the whole body is defiled, the mind too is defiled and corrupted. Paul spoke well:
"men corrupted in mind"; "evil counsel corrupts good habits."
Seek Paul, as Thecla did, so that you may hear that saying from Paul: "You need wings; if you do not have them, you have made your vow in vain."
Let that eye cry out which dwells within in purity. Let your eyes look downward, so that your mind may be above.
Great vigilance is needed, for that enemy of ours is wary. He drove us out of that paradise on earth, and now he watches us as we ascend to heaven.
See that you do not perhaps mix water into wine. In place of bread have the books of God, and in place of wine the teaching of the Savior.
Listen to the one who said: "I want you to be free from care," "and do not be anxious about anything at all except the Kingdom."
But as a person of this earth, let your heart long for heaven. Make your flesh lean, so that you may fly up along that road to heaven.
If a horse eats much, it does not run. A valiant man does not eat what he would like, so that he may not fall.
"If Israel had not eaten, he would not have wept." Let your eyes be always above, where the longed-for Lord is.
By longing for the Lord, overcome the passions. Let your prayers and your fasts help you, and let books become your comforter.
Whoever is faint-hearted in the contest never becomes crowned. Here you have a pledge of that rest.
You have not had to bear the drunkenness of your spouse. You do not weep because your child has died, or another because he has fallen ill.
You are not anxious about children, and you are set apart for the contest. Follow your Lord, who will bring you into his Kingdom.
Choose to follow the one who said: "If you walk toward me uprightly, I too will walk toward you uprightly;
if you walk toward me crookedly, I too will walk toward you crookedly in my wrath." Always wait for your Lord who is coming.
Behold, the one who said, "He will delay," is cut asunder; and the one who does not expect the coming one at all, what will he suffer?
If you want to become like Christ, follow in his footsteps. "Narrow is the gate, and only the righteous enter by it."
Hear Daniel, how he said: "I, Daniel, mourned, and for three weeks I ate no bread, and wine did not enter my mouth."
"John dwelt in the desert" and he had no vineyard, so that he would not have to toil for himself. He was a lamp, and for this reason he shut the outlets of the winds.
Remember these teachings. "Choose the heavenly life,"
"fight the good fight of faith," and in your fighting look to the victory, and in the victory look to the crown, and in the crown, to God.
Know this alone, and let your course be reverent, for "it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God." See where the images of kings are.
Some have long faces, and some have flat and handsome ones, and some have faces that are sorrowful and [?] and laughable. So too there, for we shall all appear in one image.
Flee from that shame and from that eternal trembling, and say:
"Keep me, O Lord, for I trust in you, for you have no need of my goods." Not for anyone else, but for ourselves we beseech you and for our life.
"Now let us offer ourselves as a living sacrifice, as it is written."
Not by fire, but by long-suffering, for whoever endures will be saved forever, and further, whoever has labored will be saved for all ages.
Now let us choose an unshaken and unwavering life. Let us run well, so that we may reach the goal, as it is written, "for the affliction is not small."
What you have confessed, keep. Now train your tongue and train your eyes, and stretch out your hands in purity in prayer.
Move your feet, as the Lord made you, adorned with all things.
Be modest in meeting others, unshaken in your course, ordered in eating, courageous in endurance, hardworking in this life, humble and compassionate,
loving your brothers and strong in faith, joyful, and by no means ever forget that fearful torment.
All this is said in few words, but the discipline it orders is great, as it has been said:
"The kingdom of heaven is like virgins," not like the sun, nor the moon, nor the stars, nor perishable gold, nor withering beauty, nor even the sky.
Now what does the kingdom have, which is greater than all things and free from care?
Concerning this Paul teaches us and says: "I want you to be free from care."
Now it is right to pray always, if anyone is sick, that he may revive and remain in life and not fall into suffering.
Now pray with holy David and say: "Seven times a day I praise you, O God, for the judgments of your righteousness."
It is good when in prayer we converse with God always.
If a person is edified by conversation with a good man, how much more those who converse with God day and night?
Let anyone know that God sees their sins; and now, so that sin may not break in through that forgetfulness [?].
Remember the one who said: "Pray always."
It is good to pray with the mouth, and better is prayer with the heart, for it becomes incense for you before God.
Discipline yourself beforehand and await death. Put to death your members that are on earth, for the day of the Lord comes like a thief.
If it comes and snatches your soul from you, then you will begin to say, "Give me time, so that I may fast, show mercy and repent," and the Lord will say to you:
"Did I not tell you, 'Show mercy, so that you may be shown mercy'? Or did you not hear, 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near'?
Did you not hear this saying of Paul: 'While we still have this time, let us do good'?"
For those who desire salvation have no need of much time, since that robber was not justified through much time: he believed, and he gained that inexhaustible treasure of the kingdom.
The holy martyrs were justified in a single moment, when they gave their blood; but you, instead of blood, shed tears.
He who said, "I desire the salvation of all people," does not lie.
Not only does he teach us from the holy books, but he also teaches us through other trials.
For this reason the physician treats the parts of the body [?], cuts with the blade and burns with fire, and rulers sit high on the throne and judge and punish,
so that from those evils of others we may come to repentance, so that we may be made firm in the faith and come to knowledge,
and through knowledge come to love, and from there to the inheritance, and so that we may put away sins and put on that adornment of habit.
"Let us be watchful in prayer," as it is written. Who has ever been watchful and come to harm?
Surely the shepherd stays watchful until the coming of the wolf, and the dogs lie round about, even though the beast has not come.
So vigilance is altogether good. Even if there is no reward for the labors, discipline will do you no harm, but rather it will become for you a pledge [?] of salvation.
Now listen to the good counsel of bodily fathers and mothers, who are more wrathful [?] in spirit and suffer harm along with the weak, and who say:
"Who is weak, and I am not weak?" Now it is right to apply a remedy to that saying.
The soul that has once seen sin and has remained hard-hearted has added great sickness to its flesh.
As a spark is kindled and burns up everything, so too is the nature of sin. When a thought attaches itself to the soul and there is no one
to quench it, but rather it grows stronger, that second addition is hard to heal, and it leads on all the more to contempt.
In this way many people, many times, did not quench at the outset that furnace of kindled fire, and they fell into great ruin,
for they had no one to stand against sin face to face and hinder it. It has become like a horse that breaks its bridle and throws its rider down a cliff.
So too the sick, before the coming of the physician, have great hope of life, and when the mind is taken from them [?],
from then on they are healed by no one, for they become incurably ill, not by the nature of the disease, but by their own negligence.
The corruption of sin is like a hard-mouthed [?] horse, which pulls the wrong way.
So too, after the end of this world there is no occasion for righteousness, just as with those valiant ones, who, when the contest has passed, are awarded [?] the crown.
And now the glory of the crown has been snatched away from us, so let us flee from reproach. Burning is better than reproach.
"He whose works are burned up will suffer loss," but concerning reproach I would say even more: it would be better for us to be burned with fire.
And now, if we wish that no one should reproach us, let us reproach no one, for it has been said:
"Do not reproach a man who has turned back from sins." If an adulterer bears affliction and disgrace, and yet his reproach is never wiped away,
how much more before that Judge, from whom no one can be saved even by a bribe?
Open your mouth for the word of God, and not to speak a word for useless talk.
If an account must be given for a useless word, how much more for deeds, which have come about word by word [?].
Let not the sweetness that we see deceive us; just as no one can grasp a shadow, so too are the affairs of men,
some of which come to their end and are dissolved, and some of which, even before reaching their end, pass away more swiftly than any river.
But the things of the world to come know no change, do not know old age, and have no one who alters them; rather they flourish and remain forever in the same beauty.
Do not admire riches, which do not stay with those who acquire them, but which they hand over to their own masters,
and they pass from this one to another and from that one to yet another. All this must be despised, and it is enough for you to listen to him who said:
"What we see is temporal, and what we do not see is eternal." For it is written:
"God is a righteous judge, strong and long-suffering." Great caution is needed, so that we may become like that robber on the right,
"for your enemy the devil desires your stumbling, so that you may not ascend to the place from which he fell."
"Many are his nets, and so flee from the net and the snares of the devil," so that you may say,
"for he has delivered me from the net of the hunters and from the terrifying word."
You need not only a lamp, but also light for the sake of those who watch you from afar.
You have feet and yet cannot walk unless you have the law as a light.
You have hands and yet cannot work unless light comes. You have eyes and yet cannot see unless light appears.
You travel a road day after day; you need light, so that you may not fall into a pit or fall into the hands of robbers.
Be always above the snare, and cry out: "I would dwell upon the mountains like a sparrow,"
"and who will give me wings like a dove's, and I will fly away and be at rest."
Nature has been likened to the pupil of the eye, so that the pupil may be like a maiden, and between the two eyelids,
as in a chamber, it is shut in; just as it has shut in the tongue behind two walls, the teeth and the lips,
so that, like a fearful maiden, it may say nothing better [?], but may rather foresee that judgment and say:
What will that river of fire be like, or what will that outer darkness be like, and what will that gnashing of teeth be like?
Consider all this and be pleasing to God. The Bridegroom has set out on a journey. Keep him in your mind until he comes in his glory.
Sing psalms and say: "My soul is always in your hands, and I have not forgotten your law."
As long as you are above the snare, never fall into the trap, so that you may be able to say: "My soul was delivered from the trap of the hunters."
Always fear that Judge, and if you do not desire to rest with the angels, fear being with the demons.
See, death will come just like a thief. Light your lamp and let your light shine always, so that you may not be found asleep.
Do not think about negligence, but about boldness; not about wounds, but about victory; not about the [?] of the burden, but about honor;
not about those who have fallen, but about those who have been pleasing to the crown; let there not be coals of earth within [?], but pledges of heaven.
The martyrs gave up their souls, so let us offer fasting to him. The sleep of the night seems sweet to you, but be a singer of psalms, for nothing is sweeter than psalmody.
Lying on the ground is hard for you. Understand that the martyrs were laid on burning coals.
Fasting has made your mouth bitter, but he who created the sweetness of honey drank gall for you.
You weep for yourself, but Paul the apostle wept for the salvation of others.
With this also entreat him, for the labor lasts a short time and the rest is forever and ever, for to him belong glory and honor and worship,
to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen. Christ, have mercy on Saba.
